 Another potential blow for families struggling to put food on the table. The Trump administration is proposing new restrictions to SNAP benefits, commonly known as food stamps.
 The USDA estimates 6.3 million Americans could lose assistance under the proposal.
 In Alabama, roughly 740,000 people are currently receiving SNAP benefits each month. Food banks like Feeding the Gulf Coast are concerned about what could come next.
 "Well, really, it's where do they turn?" Feeding the Gulf Coast CEO Michael Ledger asked. "One of those places is to our food bank and the amazing partners that we work with every single day that are out there getting the food to the folks that need it."
 Congress already approved major SNAP changes last year, including expanded work requirements. Now, the administration is proposing another change. It would restrict a policy known as broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which makes it easier for certain households already receiving other assistance to qualify for SNAP. Alabama is among the states using that policy.
 "That BBCE helps it make it simpler for people who are already receiving other benefits to get this benefit," Ledger said. "Sort of if you qualify for this, well, then we assume you qualify for SNAP. If they get rid of that, now they're going to have to make sure all those people that are currently sort of getting that pass, if you will."
 Ledger says Feeding the Gulf Coast distributed a record 45 million pounds of food last year, the equivalent of about 37 million meals. That's roughly double what the organization distributed six or seven years ago. He warns even that growth isn't enough to replace federal assistance if more families lose benefits.
 "It's still finite. It can't replace a federal program like SNAP," Ledger said. "So, while we're working our very hardest to try to meet that need, our real concern is that our ability will not be able to match meal for meal what SNAP can provide for every meal we provide, SNAP provides 9, and while we can scale to some degree, as we just did with this disaster, the hurricane that hit, it's still a finite resource."
 With the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays approaching, Ledger says the need for food assistance remains high.
 Feeding the Gulf Coast is continuing its food distribution efforts while helping families apply for SNAP and navigate eligibility changes through its outreach team.
 The new federal proposal is not final yet, and the public has until December 10th to comment.
